title: 'Any Sport Needs Its Heroes': Dravid Challenges Gambhir's War on Superstar Culture
excerpt: The former India coach makes the case for celebrating individual brilliance — a pointed contrast to his successor's egalitarian experiment
body:
Rahul Dravid has never been one for controversy. The man they called The Wall built an entire career — and a beloved coaching tenure — on the virtues of patience, preparation, and letting results do the talking. So when Dravid publicly contradicted his successor Gautam Gambhir's much-discussed war on "superstar culture" in Indian cricket this week, the cricketing world paid attention.

"Any sport needs its heroes," Dravid said in a wide-ranging interview, pushing back against Gambhir's oft-stated philosophy that Indian cricket should move away from individual-centric thinking. "You can't become a hero, you can't become a legend, unless you have the performances to back it up. And those performances also include your team winning."

The statement is a careful but unmistakable rebuke. Since taking over as India's head coach in late 2024, Gambhir has repeatedly emphasised collective identity over individual stardom — a philosophy that gained urgency after the retirements of Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma from Test cricket and the end of R. Ashwin's international career. But India's results under Gambhir have been mixed at best: a whitewash in Australia, no World Test Championship final appearance in the current cycle, and a sense among pundits that the team has lost more than just personnel.

## The argument for stars

Dravid's position is rooted in Indian cricket's own history. "Look at any era of Indian cricket that was successful," he argued. "Sunil Gavaskar, Kapil Dev, Sachin Tendulkar, Sourav Ganguly, Virat Kohli — the team did well when individuals were performing at an extraordinary level. That's not a coincidence."

The distinction Dravid draws is between unchecked ego and performance-driven leadership. A superstar culture that produces match-winning innings and series-defining bowling spells is, in his view, a feature, not a bug. The problem arises only when stardom becomes detached from on-field contribution — when the aura matters more than the average.

It is a nuanced argument, and one that implicitly questions whether Gambhir's approach has over-corrected. Under Dravid's own coaching, India won the 2024 T20 World Cup and reached the 2023 ODI World Cup final — campaigns built explicitly around the brilliance of Kohli, Rohit, and Jasprit Bumrah. The superstar culture, in those instances, delivered.

## Gambhir's counter

Gambhir's perspective is not without merit. His argument, articulated across multiple press conferences and interviews since taking charge, is that Indian cricket's dependency on two or three names created fragility. When Kohli had a lean patch, the batting order collapsed. When Rohit retired, there was no ready-made replacement at the top. The "no-superstar" policy is, in Gambhir's framing, about building a system robust enough to survive individual decline.

There is evidence for this view too. Australia's dominant Test sides of the 2000s were built on a deep, interchangeable squad rather than on one or two irreplaceable figures. England's white-ball revolution under Eoin Morgan deliberately flattened hierarchies. And India's current challenge — replacing Kohli, Rohit, and Ashwin simultaneously in red-ball cricket — is precisely the kind of crisis that a star-dependent system creates.

## The diaspora's stake

For NRI cricket fans, this debate is more than tactical. The superstars of Indian cricket — Tendulkar, Kohli, Dhoni — were cultural ambassadors who connected the diaspora to home. Cricket fandom in the US, UK, and Canada is often organised around these towering personalities. The question of whether Indian cricket can sustain its emotional hold on 30 million overseas Indians without transcendent individual stars is genuinely open.

The IPL, which runs on star power more than any other cricket competition, offers a partial answer. Franchises market individual players — not team identities — and the league's global growth has been driven by the magnetism of names like Kohli, Dhoni, and now Gill. A faceless Indian cricket team might win more consistently, but it could struggle to command the diaspora's attention in a crowded sports marketplace.

## The road ahead

Dravid, characteristically, did not frame his comments as an attack on Gambhir. He acknowledged that building the next generation — with players like Shubman Gill, Yashasvi Jaiswal, and the emerging crop of IPL talent — required a different approach than managing established stars. "I'm not saying you should create superstars artificially," he clarified. "I'm saying that when someone earns that status through performance, the system should celebrate it, not suppress it."

The tension between these two visions — Gambhir's egalitarian project and Dravid's belief in the necessity of heroes — will define Indian cricket's trajectory over the next World Cup cycle. With the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa and the 2028 T20 World Cup in India on the horizon, the stakes extend beyond philosophy. Indian cricket needs both a system and stars. The question is which comes first.
